Jean de l'Espine
zhahn de les-peen'
n. (Jean de l'Espine, c. 1506–1597, Huguenot pastor at Angers and writer on the quiet of the Christian mind)
French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; de l'Espine, of the thorn.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jean de l'Espine was an Augustinian who came out to the Reformed faith in middle life, pastored at Angers and elsewhere through the whole span of the French religious wars, and lived to be ninety. His best books are not polemics but treatises on the inward life: on the tranquillity of the mind, on patience in affliction, on the right use of the Lord's Supper, written for people whose churches were burned and whose relatives had been killed. The dictionary values that choice of subject. A pastor in a civil war is tempted to write only about the war. L'Espine wrote about how a Christian keeps a quiet mind when he has lost his property and buried his friends, and he wrote it as a man who had lived the question rather than as a man proposing a technique. The result is Reformed devotional writing of the first rank, and it is the opposite of what the therapeutic age means by self-care: the quiet he describes comes from outside the self, from God's decree and Christ's finished work, and not from managing one's feelings.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines tranquillity as quietness and calmness of mind, and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm temper.

expand to see more

TRANQUIL'LITY, n. Quietness; a calm state; freedom from disturbance or agitation of mind.

PA'TIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.

AFFLIC'TION, n. The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief.

CONSOLA'TION, n. Comfort; alleviation of misery or distress of mind.

Key Scripture

Isa 26:3 — "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee."

Joh 14:27 — "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."

Phi 4:7 — "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus."

Rom 5:3 — "And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;"

Modern Corruption

He wrote on the quiet Christian mind for people whose churches were burned, and grounded it outside the self.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the therapeutic redefinition of peace. Modern self-help teaches that calm is a skill: regulate the feeling, reframe the thought, and the mind quiets itself. L'Espine, writing to congregations under arms, located peace somewhere no technique can reach — in the God who keeps the mind stayed on Him, and in a reconciliation already accomplished and not dependent on how the Christian happens to feel this week. The two accounts look similar from a distance and are opposite at the root: one makes the self the source of its own rest, the other receives rest as a gift.

The standard is the biblical one. “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee” (Isa 26:3). The peace is Christ's own and is not the world's kind: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you” (Joh 14:27). It passes explanation and does the guarding itself — “the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus” (Phi 4:7) — and tribulation is not its enemy but its school: “we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience” (Rom 5:3).

Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness; Greek eirene (G1515), peace.

Hebrew samak (H5564) — to lean, to uphold, to stay; Isaiah 26:3.

Greek eirene (G1515) — peace; John 14:27.

Usage

"“whose mind is stayed on thee” (Isa 26:3) — a treatise on tranquillity written during the wars."

"“not as the world giveth, give I unto you” (Joh 14:27) — peace grounded outside the self."

"“tribulation worketh patience” (Rom 5:3) — ninety years, most of them in a divided France."
